analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to pay cash compensation, rebooking, meals, and hotels when their own delays strand passengers.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 17 senators (15 Democrats and 1 independent) with no Republicans, has sat in the Senate Commerce Committee since its introduction in December 2025 with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When an airline cancels a flight or delays it badly and the airline itself is at fault, this bill would require the airline to pay each passenger cash compensation (at least $750 while an interim rule is in effect, with a longer-term structure modeled on Canadian and European rules of $300 for delays over 3 hours and $600 for 6 or more), rebook the passenger for free on any carrier, provide a meal, and cover a hotel and ground transportation for overnight cancellations. The Transportation Department would first convene a committee with airlines, airports, and consumer groups to recommend details, then write binding rules on a deadline, reporting to Congress every 6 months until the final rule is done.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers whose trips are ruined by delays or cancellations the airline itself caused. In 2024's summer travel and the December 2022 Southwest meltdown, passengers were often left with no compensation at all; this bill would put money, rebooking, meals, and hotel rooms in their pockets automatically. It applies to foreign carriers flying US routes too, so travelers on international itineraries are covered.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Passengers hit by controllable airline disruptions

how_it_helps.text: Requires $750 in cash compensation per passenger for cancellations or significant delays directly attributable to the airline, under an interim rule that must take effect within 2 years of enactment.
Requires free rebooking on the same or any other carrier, or an alternative means of transportation, at no additional cost to the passenger.
Requires a meal or meal credit for affected passengers, plus complimentary hotel accommodations and ground transportation for overnight cancellations.

Directs the Transportation Department to model longer-term compensation on Canadian and European passenger-protection rules, which set minimums of $300 for delays over 3 hours and $600 for delays of 6 or more hours.

Requires the Department to make the compensation and reimbursement process clear, simple, and prompt, and to educate passengers on what they are owed, addressing the fact that most travelers never claim compensation they are entitled to today.
Requires the Secretary of Transportation to report to Congress every 6 months on rulemaking progress until a final rule is issued, creating public accountability for delays.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, which would pay compensation, rebooking, meals, and hotel costs out of revenue when their own operations cause disruptions. That cost would likely flow partly into fares for all travelers and partly into airline margins. Weather delays, air traffic control problems, and other disruptions not attributable to the airline are excluded, so the cost is limited to controllable cancellations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Airlines, and travelers through higher fares

drawbacks.text: Airline costs ultimately come from passengers: compensation requirements are widely passed through to ticket prices, so infrequent travelers effectively subsidize payouts to frequent ones, and the industry warns the added cost burden lands on consumers.

The bill does not take effect for up to 2 years after enactment, and even then only through an interim rule that lasts until a final rule is issued following a committee report and proposed rulemaking, so stranded passengers get nothing for years.

Compensation applies only when a disruption is 'directly attributable' to the airline, and the process for determining that is left to a committee to recommend, creating a likely battleground over every weather-adjacent delay.

The flat $750 interim payment can exceed the actual harm in some cases (a $150 ticket delayed 4 hours) and undercompensate in others (a business traveler missing a closed deal), which is the trade-off of a simple bright-line rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one in four flyers who experiences a controllable cancellation or long delay, the bill delivers real, automatic cash and support in the worst moment of travel, where today most get nothing. The cost is real but modest relative to airline industry revenue, and it is paid mostly by the airlines whose failures caused the disruption. The main fair criticism is the long runway: a committee process, then a proposed rule, then an interim rule in 2 years, then a final rule. Passengers see nothing until then, and airlines have every incentive to slow that timeline.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has not held a hearing or taken any action on it, and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Kelly introduced the bill on December 4, 2025, with 16 original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

All 16 cosponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican senators have signed on, which matters because the Senate Commerce Committee and the Senate floor generally require some bipartisan support to move legislation.
No further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no vote — has been recorded since the referral, and Congress remains in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has been hurt and no one has won: the bill simply sits. Airlines and airports, who would bear the new costs, are better off with it stalled in committee, and the 17 sponsoring senators are better off politically than they would be with an actual vote on record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines, so far — the bill has gone nowhere

for.name: Sen. Mark Kelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on December 4, 2025, and saw it referred to the Commerce Committee.

for.name: 16 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Blumenthal, Markey, Sanders, Klobuchar, Booker, and Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors the day of introduction, giving the bill a fully Democratic or independent slate of supporters.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Major U.S. airlines and their trade group Airlines for America
against.what_they_did: Have publicly opposed mandatory cash compensation rules, arguing costs are passed to consumers; they fought similar Transportation Department proposals.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors are Democrats or an independent; no Republican senator has signed on, and the bill's fate now rests with a committee where the majority party controls the calendar.

industries.note: Airlines would owe $750 per passenger plus meals, hotels, and rebooking on any carrier whenever their own operations strand travelers — a direct, recurring cash cost with no offsetting benefit. Foreign carriers flying US routes are covered too. Airline interest in this bill runs squarely against the passengers it protects.

Airport operators sit on the rulemaking committee that will shape the rules, and stranded-passenger rules can change rebooking patterns and gate congestion at hub airports, but the bill imposes no direct requirements on them.
A mandated airline-paid compensation and rebooking right makes some paid disruption insurance and fee-based rebooking services less necessary; this cost shift favors ordinary travelers.

analysis.trajectory: This bill has been in committee for months with no hearing or vote and no Republican support, which is the profile of a bill that dies quietly at the end of the two-year Congress. The realistic path to any passenger compensation rule runs through the Transportation Department's own rulemaking rather than legislation, and even a DOT rule can be undone by a future administration — which is exactly the gap this bill was written to close and, so far, has not been able to.
